Lesson 4.1

Game Engines: Input, Simulation, and Rendering

The previous chapters followed values into instructions and turned remote bytes into typed objects and collections. The next question is larger: which system moves them, resolves collisions, applies damage, and advances timers? A health update might be native code, a cooldown calculation a script, and a unit’s starting health loaded from a data file. Finding the relevant function or definition starts with separating game-specific behavior from the engine services that execute it.

The game loop reads input, checks whether actions are allowed, updates positions and health, and draws the result. Games need other machinery too: something loads the level, stores objects, and calls the renderer. A game engine supplies much of this reusable machinery. Knowing where it stops and the game begins tells you which technique in this book will work on a given problem.

An engine is reusable game machinery

Section titled “An engine is reusable game machinery”

Many games need the same kinds of machinery, even when their weapons, maps, and art are different:

  • a game loop that reads input, updates the world, and draws a frame, over and over (Lesson 1.3);
  • a renderer that turns the world into pixels;
  • a way to load art, sound, levels, and settings from disk;
  • a model of the world: what objects exist, where they are, what they hold;
  • collision, when objects can meet walls or one another;
  • sound, input, menus, and sometimes networking and scripting.

Not every game needs every item: a text adventure may have no renderer or collision system. For games that do need these pieces, reusing them can save substantial work. A game about tanks and a game about farming can share the window, input, loading, and rendering machinery while supplying different behavior: armor damage for tanks, crop growth for farming.

A game engine is that reusable machinery: the software that runs the loop, draws the frames, loads the files, and manages the objects, on which a particular game’s content and behavior—such as what a hit does or what a unit costs—are built.

A spreadsheet program is a useful comparison, because it holds up when you push on it. The program supplies the grid, the formulas, and the recalculation; each spreadsheet file supplies its own numbers and formulas. A bug in how the program recalculates breaks every spreadsheet you open. A wrong formula in one file breaks only that file. And two files made in the same program share the same structure, so once you understand one, the next is easier to read. All three statements hold for engines and games too, which is exactly what makes the split worth learning.

Who calls whom

Section titled “Who calls whom”

Games also use libraries. A useful first distinction is who controls the main loop and calls whose code.

Your code calls a library. SDL, for example, is a library that Wesnoth’s engine uses to open a window, read the keyboard, and play sound. It has no idea what a unit or a map is; it waits to be asked.

An engine often calls your code. It may own the loop and call the game’s update and draw functions at the moments it chooses. The game is a guest in a loop the engine runs. Those update and draw functions are callbacks: the game hands them to the engine, and the engine decides when to run them.

This is a way to reason about control flow, not a rigid test for what a project may call an engine. Engine code can call libraries, and game code can call engine functions too.

Outside games, software that works this way is called a framework. A web framework owns the loop that waits for requests and calls the handler you registered for each address, so the same question — who calls whom — sorts those tools too.

Alternative: A library is a toolbox you reach into when you need it. An engine is more like a stage manager who calls your cue when it is your turn.

This matters later in a practical way. A repeated call near frame presentation can be a useful meeting point when you verify that the game actually reaches it. That is why Lesson 7.10 hooks Present: this game’s rendering path calls it to show finished frames, making it a good place to observe them.

Starting up: plugins and settings

Section titled “Starting up: plugins and settings”

Before the first frame, the application starts up. It reads its settings from a file, such as the resolution, the volume, and the key bindings. It creates the window, and it sets up each part of the engine. Engines package those parts as plugins. A plugin is a module that registers what it needs, such as its systems and the event types it uses, with the application when it is added, and a plugin group adds several together, such as the window, the input, the renderer, and the audio. The game itself is then a small plugin of its own, and swapping one plugin, say for a different renderer, changes one part without touching the rest. Changed settings are written back to the file, so they persist the way a save does (Chapter 9).

One frame, step by step

Section titled “One frame, step by step”

An engine that owns the loop does the same few jobs on every pass through it, in the same order:

  1. Gather input. Ask the operating system which keys, buttons, and mouse movements happened since the last pass, and turn them into actions (Lesson 1.3).
  2. Update the world. Move objects, resolve contacts, apply damage, count timers down, and choose character actions.
  3. Draw. Build the picture of the world as it is now.
  4. Present. Hand the finished picture to the display, and, with vertical sync on, wait for the display’s next refresh.

Frame time and frame rate are reciprocals of each other:

tframe=1000fps mst_{\text{frame}} = \frac{1000}{\text{fps}}\ \text{ms}tframe​=fps1000​ ms

A display that refreshes 60 times each second takes a new picture every 1 ÷ 60 = 0.01667 seconds, which is 16.67 milliseconds. All four jobs must fit in that frame budget, or the display refreshes before the new picture is ready and shows the old one again. A frame that takes 25 ms gives 1 ÷ 0.025 = 40 frames per second; one that takes 8.33 ms gives 120. This is why tools report frame time, in milliseconds, as well as frames per second. Frame times add up, so a 4 ms update plus a 10 ms draw is a 14 ms frame, but frame rates do not add.

Time inside the update

Section titled “Time inside the update”

Lesson 1.3 showed that movement needs elapsed time: distance = speed × time. An engine measures the delta time, the seconds since the previous frame, and hands it to every update. Physics prefers steady steps, though. If one frame moves a fast ball 3 pixels and the next moves it 30, a contact test that looks only at positions can jump the ball clean over a wall 10 pixels thick. So many engines run physics in a fixed timestep, such as 1/60 second, and carry the leftover real time into the next frame:

ExampleThree frames of fixed steps

Frame Real time since the last frame (ms) Time waiting to be simulated (ms) Fixed steps run (16.67 ms each) Left over (ms)
1 20.00 0 + 20.00 = 20.00 1 20.00 − 16.67 = 3.33
2 20.00 3.33 + 20.00 = 23.33 1 23.33 − 16.67 = 6.67
3 30.00 6.67 + 30.00 = 36.67 2 36.67 − 33.33 = 3.33

After 70 ms of real time the game has run 4 steps, which is 4 × 16.67 = 66.67 ms of game time, and 3.33 ms is waiting. The two add back to 70 ms, so no time was lost. A slow frame runs several steps to catch up, and a quick one runs none.

A game loop turning frames into fixed steps. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

STEP = 1000 / 60;  waiting = 0  # ms of game time per step
each frame, real_ms has passed:
    waiting = waiting + real_ms
    while waiting >= STEP:
        run_one_step()  # rules advance by STEP
        waiting = waiting - STEP
    draw()  # blend by what is left

After 70.00 ms of real time the game ran 4 steps, which is 66.67 ms of game time, with 3.33 ms waiting. 66.67 + 3.33 = 70.00 ms, so no time was lost.

Final values: STEP = 16.67 ms; waiting = 3.33 ms; steps_run = 4; frame = 3; real_ms = 30.00 ms; game_time = 66.67 ms; blend = 20%.

What is drawn after a frame is usually partway between two steps. The 3.33 ms left over is 3.33 ÷ 16.67 = 20% of the way to the next step, and many engines blend the last two steps by that fraction, so motion looks smooth even though the simulation advances in fixed steps (Lesson 4.4 shows how that blend is computed).

This tells you something when you scan memory. A value the simulation changes moves once per step, and a value the drawing code keeps (an on-screen animation timer, an interpolated position) can change once per frame. Counting how often a value changes tells you which loop owns it.

A cooldown is a timer built the same way. When an ability is used, the game stores how long remains, say 5.0 seconds, and subtracts the delta time on every step: after 60 steps of 1/60 second the value has fallen by 1.0 to 4.0, and after 300 steps it reaches 0 and the ability is ready. Some games instead store the moment it becomes ready (now + 5.0) and compare it with the clock. Either way the cooldown is a number in memory that you can scan for.

Real time, game time, and the clamp

Section titled “Real time, game time, and the clamp”

The delta time an update receives is not always the time that really passed. Engines keep two clocks. Real time is the wall clock (Explanation: The time a clock on a wall shows. It keeps running whatever the game does, so pausing the game cannot stop it.): it never stops, and a loading spinner or a menu animation uses it. Game time is the clock used for simulated movement and cooldowns. Each frame the engine takes the real time since the last frame, limits it to a maximum, and multiplies it by a time scale:

Δgame=min⁡(Δreal, Δmax⁡)×s\Delta_{\text{game}} = \min(\Delta_{\text{real}},\ \Delta_{\max}) \times sΔgame​=min(Δreal​, Δmax​)×s

A scale of 1 is normal speed, 0.5 is slow motion, 2 is fast forward, and 0 is a pause. A pause stops game time but not real time, which is why a paused game still draws its menu and answers the mouse. The scale also stretches every timer that counts game time:

ExampleOne 16.67 ms frame at four time scales

Time scale Game time added by the frame A 5.0 s cooldown ends after
1 (normal) 16.67 ms 5.0 ÷ 1 = 5.0 s of real time
0.5 (slow motion) 16.67 × 0.5 = 8.33 ms 5.0 ÷ 0.5 = 10.0 s
2 (fast forward) 16.67 × 2 = 33.33 ms 5.0 ÷ 2 = 2.5 s
0 (paused) 0 ms never, while paused

The limit bounds the simulation time added after a stalled frame. A laptop that sleeps, or a window held still by the mouse for 3 seconds, would otherwise hand the next update a delta of 3.0 s. A ball moving 150 pixels a second would jump 150 × 3.0 = 450 pixels at once, straight through any wall, and a fixed-step loop would owe 3.0 ÷ (1/60) = 180 steps. Bevy’s default limit is 250 ms, so the longest delta any frame can add is 0.25 s, and at 60 steps a second the loop owes at most 0.25 ÷ (1/60) = 15 steps.

The limit also ends a failure called the spiral of death. Suppose each fixed step takes 20 ms of real time to compute but advances game time by only 16.67 ms. While the engine computes one step, the real clock moves 20 ms, so the next frame owes 20 ms of game time, which is 20 ÷ 16.67 = 1.2 times as much as the step paid off. The frame after that owes 1.2 times as much again. Each step leaves the game 20 − 16.67 = 3.33 ms further behind real time, so after 60 steps it is 60 × 3.33 = 200 ms behind, and running more steps to catch up only adds more debt. The clamp throws the excess away, so the game falls behind real time and runs in slow motion instead of freezing.

Scanning memory is easier with this in mind. A game’s elapsed time may exist twice: one value that always rises, and one that stops during a pause. A cooldown that compares itself with the second pauses with the game, and one that compares itself with the first keeps running behind the pause menu.

Slow work leaves the frame

Section titled “Slow work leaves the frame”

Reading a 3 MB file can take 30 ms. If the update waited for it, the game would miss 30 ÷ 16.67 = 1.8, so two, refreshes. Engines give slow jobs, such as loading files, decoding sound, or planning a path across a big map, to worker threads (Lesson 6.6) as tasks. The main loop starts a task and keeps running frames. When the task finishes, it sends its result through a channel, a queue that one thread fills and another empties, and the main loop checks the channel once per frame.

The result arrives on a frame nobody can predict, so the game has to handle “not ready yet” with a loading screen or a stand-in. Lesson 6.11 uses the same channel to move records from a game to a recorder without stalling it.

Measuring the frame

Section titled “Measuring the frame”

Engines measure themselves. A diagnostic is a named measurement with a short history, such as frame time over the last 120 frames, that can be switched on and off while the game runs. An FPS overlay draws such numbers on the screen. A log records events as lines of text, each with a severity such as error, warning, info, or debug, to a console or a file.

An average can hide a stutter. Four frames of 16, 16, 16, and 66 ms average (16 + 16 + 16 + 66) ÷ 4 = 28.5 ms, or 1000 ÷ 28.5 = 35 frames per second, even though three frames in four were fine. The 66 ms frame is the one a player feels, so a good diagnostic also reports the slowest frame.

Narration: Players feel the one slow frame, not the average. That is why frame-time graphs show spikes that a single frames-per-second number hides.

The build changes the measurement as much as the code does. A debug build leaves out most optimizations so that mistakes are easier to find, and engine code that loops over thousands of entities can run many times slower in it than in a release build. Suppose a system takes 0.4 ms in a release build and 12 ms in a debug build. That is 12 ÷ 0.4 = 30 times slower, and 12 ms alone is 12 ÷ 16.67 = 72% of the frame budget. A frame time means little until you know which kind of build produced it.

Entities, components, and systems

Section titled “Entities, components, and systems”

Lesson 1.3 gave things identities, and Lesson 3.10 showed an engine keeping each kind of field in its own collection. Many engines make that the whole design. In an entity component system (ECS):

  • an entity is only an identity, a number (with a generation, so a reused number is told apart from the old one, as Lesson 3.10 explained);
  • a component is a plain bundle of data attached to an entity, such as Position, Velocity, or Health;
  • a system is a function that runs on every update for all the entities that have a particular set of components.

A movement system says: for every entity with both Position and Velocity, add velocity × delta time to position. A wall has a Position but no Velocity, so the movement system never touches it, and nobody wrote an “if wall” test. What an entity does comes from which components it has, not from what kind of object it is.

Alternative: Think of a school: students are just ID numbers, clubs say what each one does, and a system is a teacher who visits everyone in the chess club.

Entity Components Movement system Collision system Draw system
tank Position, Velocity, Size, Sprite runs runs runs
wall Position, Size, Sprite skips runs runs
coin Position, Size, Sprite, Pickup skips runs runs
hidden trigger Position, Size skips runs skips

In memory, each kind of component sits in its own run. Ten thousand Position components of two 4-byte floats each take 10,000 × 8 = 80,000 bytes in one stretch, which is what Lesson 3.10 called a component pool. A system walks that stretch from start to end, and a scan finds the whole run at once.

Entity updates also need coordination:

  • A system should not add or remove entities while it is looping over them, or the loop could skip some and visit others twice. Instead it queues commands (spawn this, despawn that, add this component), and the engine applies them together at a safe moment between systems. A delayed command is one the engine holds back until a timer ends, such as removing an effect after 2 seconds.
  • Disabling an entity hides it from the systems without deleting it. A marker component such as Disabled makes the queries skip it. Its identity and data stay in memory, so it can come back unchanged. Despawning is different: the identity is freed and may be reused.
  • An observer is code that runs when something happens, such as an entity being created, a component being removed, or “coin 42 was collected” (the event from Lesson 1.3), instead of checking every frame whether it happened.

Lesson 6.8 follows how systems share data through resources and events, how the engine decides which system runs first and which can run at the same time, and how it notices only what changed.

Scenes: a world you can load

Section titled “Scenes: a world you can load”

Once the world is made of entities, the engine needs a way to create many of them at once. A scene is a group of entities with their components that can be created together: a level, a menu screen, or one character with all its parts. A scene usually lives in a file (a data format, Chapter 9) and is spawned at run time: the engine reads the file, creates the entities, and fills in the components.

Entities in a scene can form a hierarchy. A tank can have a child for its turret and a grandchild for the gun barrel. A child’s position is stored relative to its parent, so moving the tank moves the turret and the barrel with it, and despawning the tank despawns them too. Lesson 7.1 works out how a child’s position becomes a world position.

Games also organize scenes into states: a menu, a loading screen, the match, the game-over screen. Entering a state spawns its scene, and leaving it despawns it. A loading screen waits for every file the next scene needs. It counts the files still loading, and when the count reaches 0 it switches to the match. This matters when you hunt for addresses: the entities of one scene are freed when the scene is left, so an address found in one level can mean nothing in the next.

The five course games, sorted by engine

Section titled “The five course games, sorted by engine”

The games in this book cover most of the ways a game can relate to its engine:

Game Engine Typical places to inspect behavior and configuration
Wesnoth 1.14.9 its own engine, written for this game C++ engine code, WML data files, Lua scripts
AssaultCube 1.2.0.2 Cube, an open-source engine C++ engine code
Urban Terror 4.3.4 ioquake3, the continuation of the open-sourced Quake III engine C++ engine code
Flare 1.12 Flare, an engine built to run content packages text data files
Wyrmsun 5.0.1 Wyrmgus, a fork of the Stratagus strategy engine Lua scripts and data

Flare shows the split most clearly. Flare is the engine; a campaign such as the Empyrean Campaign from Lesson 10.2 is a content package the engine loads. Swap the content package and the same executable runs a different game.

Find the source of a behavior or value

Section titled “Find the source of a behavior or value”

A spending calculation is implemented in code; a price or starting health value may come from a data file or script. Identify that source before changing a live value. It tells you which technique applies and when the game might replace your edit with a newly calculated or loaded value.

Wesnoth shows two of them side by side:

Gold during a match

A number in memory, updated by native engine code. Change it with the scan from Lesson 1.9 and it changes for this match. Start a new match and it begins from the scenario’s starting gold again.

A unit's hit points

They come from a unit definition in a WML data file. Change one unit’s hit points in memory and that single unit changes. Recruit another of the same type and it arrives with the file’s value, because every new unit is built from the definition on disk. Change the definition file instead, and units created after the game reloads that edited definition use the new value.

Choose according to whether you want to change one live unit or the definition that future units will load. That distinction explains why a memory edit can be overwritten while a reloaded definition produces the change again.

TL;DR: Changing one live unit affects that instance. Changing its type definition affects units created from it after the edited definition is loaded.

Source layer What you change Where this book covers it
a data file the file, before the game loads it Chapter 9
a script the script, or what the host lets it do Chapter 10
native engine code values in memory, or the instructions themselves Chapters 2, 3, 5, and 6
managed code, such as C# in Unity often readable by decompiling it Lesson 6.2

The data-file row deserves special attention. When a game exposes a file for customization, editing it may be the simplest route. Keep a copy of the original: a game update can still replace a file or change its format. Chapter 9 opens with this decision.

Engines leave their own tools in the game

Section titled “Engines leave their own tools in the game”

Engines are built by developers who need to debug them, and many ship with those debugging tools still inside.

The rendering lessons will use some of these tools. Lesson 7.2 uses Urban Terror’s console variables — named settings the engine exposes — to switch entity drawing on and off. Lessons 7.5 and 7.6 open AssaultCube’s console with ~ and use commands such as idlebots 1, dbgpos 1, and showstats 1 to freeze the bots and print positions on screen.

Those tools are gifts. A console variable that toggles a feature gives you a clean experiment: flip it, and whatever changes in memory is connected to that feature. A debug command that prints your position tells you what value to scan for. Check what the engine already offers before reaching for a debugger.

Overlays, gizmos, editors, and stress tests

Section titled “Overlays, gizmos, editors, and stress tests”

Other developer tools are drawn by the engine itself:

  • A debug overlay prints live numbers, such as frame time, on the screen.
  • Debug drawing, called gizmos in some engines, draws shapes for a single frame without creating any game object: a line, an arrow, a box around a collision shape, the three coloured axes of an object’s own directions, a circle for a light’s reach, a text label. The code calls something like draw_line(a, b, colour) on every frame, and when it stops calling, the shape is gone. An editor’s transform gizmo is the interactive version: three arrows you drag to move, turn, or scale a selected object. Lesson 7.9 draws the same kind of overlay over someone else’s game.
  • An editor lets designers place entities and save scenes, and draws a grid on the ground so the scale and the position of things can be read. A viewer shows one kind of data on its own, such as a 3D model or the buttons of a game controller, without running the whole game.
  • A stress test deliberately runs a heavy load, such as ten thousand sprites, and watches the frame time to find where the game breaks down. If each sprite costs 0.002 ms, 10,000 of them cost 20 ms, which is already over the 16.67 ms budget. Lesson 7.3 shows where such costs come from.

A whole game from these parts: Breakout

Section titled “A whole game from these parts: Breakout”

The parts fit together in a game small enough to hold in your head. In Breakout, a paddle at the bottom of the screen bounces a ball upward into rows of bricks.

  • Entities and components. The paddle has Position, Size, and PlayerControlled. The ball has Position, Velocity, and Size. Each of the 40 bricks has Position, Size, and Brick.
  • Systems, in order, every fixed step. Read input into the paddle’s velocity. Move everything that has a Velocity. Test the ball against the walls, the paddle, and the bricks. A hit brick is despawned by a command and adds 1 to the score. If the ball falls below the paddle, switch the game’s state to game over. After the steps, draw every entity that has a Position and a sprite.
  • State. The score, the bricks left, and the lives are numbers in memory. So is the mode: menu, playing, or game over.

ExampleOne step of Breakout

One step, with real numbers. The ball is at x = 794 with a velocity of 150 pixels per second to the right, and a step is 1/60 second:

Nothing in that step names Breakout. It is the position update and wall-collision response from Lesson 1.3 run by systems over entities, in the order the engine’s loop calls them.

Where each engine part is explained

Section titled “Where each engine part is explained”

This lesson names the parts. The lessons below explain how each one works, and the small runnable examples of an open-source engine such as Bevy (Reference: The example gallery of the Bevy engine: small programs that each show one engine part, such as sprites, lighting, audio, UI, or picking.) show nearly every one in a few dozen lines.

Engine part What it does Explained in

Recognizing an engine outside this book

Section titled “Recognizing an engine outside this book”

Most commercial games are built on a small number of large engines. Three you will meet often:

  • Unity — game logic is usually written in C#, which changes how you find data, as Lesson 6.2 explains;
  • Unreal — C++ engine code, with a visual scripting system called Blueprints;
  • Godot — an open-source engine whose games are scripted in its own GDScript language or in C#.

Games built on the same engine may share code, naming patterns, and file formats. Object layouts also depend on the game’s code and engine version, so use a familiar pattern as a clue and verify it in the next game.

Lesson 6.2 shows how to tell which engine a game uses from the files beside its executable. Do that first. It takes a minute, and it tells you which of the rows in the table above you are dealing with.

Where the change belongs

Section titled “Where the change belongs”

An engine supplies reusable machinery; the game adds its particular weapon values, damage routines, missions, and content. A library responds when your code calls it, while an engine also calls game code at the points it controls. The course games use different engines, so a health update or unit definition may live in data, a script, native code, or managed code. A memory edit lasts for a running process; a data-file edit can persist when the file is loaded again. Engine consoles and debug commands expose named state that can help identify the right layer before changing it.

To describe a match, a tool needs more than one verified field: it needs the players and values that belong together at one moment. From One Player to a Game-State Snapshot builds that view while keeping the engine’s changing state separate from the tool’s local copy.

Lesson 4.2

From One Player to a Game-State Snapshot

The engine owns and updates the match; our tool owns only the values it copies. A gold scan gives us one value for one player. In a strategy match, that is rarely enough: several sides may have the same gold while their identities and income differ. An observer has to turn verified fields into a useful view of the whole match without pretending it owns the game’s changing state.

The remaining lessons grow that observer into a model of game behavior. Snapshots and tile grids explain what the world contains; coordinates describe where it is; feedback, paths, and events explain how a tool reacts. A bounded recorder makes observations useful over time. Finally, an NPC shows how the game itself senses and chooses.

What an observer does

Section titled “What an observer does”

An observer reads state and presents it without trying to become the game’s state owner. It separates three layers:

The remote process may change immediately after the read. PlayerSnapshot is therefore a copy of the values at one moment, not a live reference into Wesnoth. This distinction keeps the rest of the program safe and makes timestamps and failed reads honest.

TL;DR: A snapshot is a copy taken at one moment. The tool works on its copy because the game keeps changing underneath it.

Note

📸 Snapshot idea: a snapshot is a photograph, not a live window. It records what the remote process looked like at one moment and may be stale a moment later.

A useful observer also has a sampling rate. Reading once per second answers strategy-level questions such as gold and income. Reading thousands of times per second adds overhead without making those slow values more truthful.

From one player to a collection

Section titled “From one player to a collection”

We already traced one player’s gold. Strategy games usually store several similar player records in an array, vector, or table.

An array places fixed-size records next to one another. A table may instead contain pointers to separately allocated records. The address pattern tells them apart:

For an illustrative inline table starting at 0x1000 with 32-byte records, player index 2 begins at 0x1040: two strides of 0x20 bytes after the base. In a pointer table, that same calculation locates a pointer slot; reading the slot gives the record address. The two layouts require different read steps.

Alternative: Picture inline records as seats in a row: seat number times seat width gives the place. A pointer table is a row of tickets, each naming a seat elsewhere.

This interactive lab needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it still explains the same idea.

The inline formula applies only once the debugger shows a consistent stride between real players.

The goal is not to guess a distance and hope. We will use two known players and the debugger to learn how the game indexes them.

Observe the income loop

Section titled “Observe the income loop”

Set a breakpoint on the gold update used at the end of a turn. Each time the instruction runs, read the object pointer it uses.

If the function loops through players, the object pointer should change while the instruction stays the same. Nearby 32-bit x86 instructions may calculate an index in this shape:

That pair is the collection indexing introduced in Lesson 1.3 and the scaled-offset formula examined in Lesson 3.10, written as two instructions. The three-operand imul multiplies the index in edx by a constant and puts the result in eax; the add then moves that distance from the table’s start. This is an illustrative shape, not a claimed byte-for-byte Wesnoth listing.

The constant is the useful part. You do not have to infer the record size by finding two players and subtracting their addresses — the instruction states it, because the compiler had to know the stride to generate this code at all. Read it off, then confirm it against two real players rather than trusting a single instruction.

This suggests:

Two known players confirm it: their record addresses should differ by exactly one record size. That difference gives the stride, not yet the complete layout of a record.

Model only confirmed fields

Section titled “Model only confirmed fields”

Do not cast an unknown memory range to a giant struct. Read confirmed fields by offset into a snapshot:

PlayerSnapshot owns copied values. It does not pretend that remote memory is a safe local reference.

The layout object keeps the offsets apart from the values read through them. gold: 4 means “gold sits four bytes from each record’s base in this build.” Storing the number does not make it true; range checks and behavior tests decide whether it still holds for this exact build.

Read until the model says stop

Section titled “Read until the model says stop”

Find the player count or another verified boundary. Never scan player records forever.

Compare that with silently skipping records that fail:

The original helper reads each player and keeps only successful rows. A failed row disappears without an error, so the returned list can look complete even when the layout is wrong or the game changed during capture.

Validate the known lab limit of sixteen players first, then collect results into one Result<Vec<_>>. Any failed read rejects the whole claimed snapshot instead of quietly shortening it.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: return a complete trusted snapshot or a visible error, rather than disguising missing rows.

Why this version?

A missing row means a bad layout, a changing process, or an unreadable record, not that the player does not exist. Collecting Result stops at the first untrusted row, so the dashboard never presents a partial table as complete. The count cap also prevents a corrupted count from turning one bad read into thousands of reads.

collect() stops on the first error and returns it with no half-trusted table.

Narration: A dashboard that quietly skips unreadable rows can look healthy while hiding a bad layout. Failing loudly shows the problem at once.

Print a useful dashboard

Section titled “Print a useful dashboard”

Once read_players has returned validated snapshots, display one line per side. The loop uses each snapshot’s slot, gold, and signed income; {:+} shows whether income adds to or drains gold. A failed read ends with an error before the dashboard can present a partial set as complete.

Refresh slowly—once or twice per second is enough for a learning tool. Constant reads waste CPU and make failures harder to follow.

Exact Wesnoth 1.14.9 stat path

Section titled “Exact Wesnoth 1.14.9 stat path”

This is the exercise the original course called the stathack.

The income breakpoint at 0x009B4CE3 reveals that Wesnoth advances through player records in steps of 0x270 bytes. The paths for the first two players are:

Those paths become a real reader:

Create a two-local-player match, end one turn for each player, and print indices 0 and 1. Spend gold with each side separately. Only the matching row should change. You have now rebuilt the original Wesnoth state observer.

Validate the snapshot

Section titled “Validate the snapshot”

For each field:

  1. observe it in the game;
  2. read it from the tool;
  3. change it through normal gameplay;
  4. confirm the tool follows;
  5. restart and re-resolve the table.

If one player has impossible values, stop and revisit the table base, record size, count, or offsets.

The key upgrade is conceptual: instead of “address plus magic number,” we now have a named layout, checked math, a bounded collection, and owned snapshots.

Lesson 4.3

Why Snapshots Need Guarded Actions

The observer in the previous lesson copied player state for display. A tool that changes state faces a harder problem: gold can change after the read but before the write. If income arrives in that gap, a blind write may overwrite it. We need a pipeline that treats every observation as temporary evidence.

One long function hides where it can fail

Section titled “One long function hides where it can fail”

A beginner tool often grows as one long function:

That can work once, but every step depends on facts collected earlier. The game may restart, change maps, end a turn, replace an object, or update the value while the tool is still running.

A more reliable tool separates six phases:

Repeated reads can expose a changing snapshot. This step-by-step trace needs JavaScript. Here is the code and where the run ends.

read the selected inputs
evaluate each stated condition
combine the required conditions
perform the effect only when accepted
otherwise retain the old state
report the result and its limits

Result: retain the current gold and recapture; the observed values did not stay stable.

Final values: income = 30; late = no; first_capture = 100; second_capture = 130; captures_agree = false; fresh_check_matches = true; accepted = false; gold_after = 130.

The important idea is not extra code. It is that data crosses a gate before the tool acts on it. A raw address read once may already be out of date. A Snapshot captured twice with equal results was consistent at that moment. A write happens only if a fresh capture, taken immediately before it, still equals the snapshot.

TL;DR: Treat every read as temporary evidence. Re-check it right before acting, and write only if nothing has changed.

Store one snapshot in one typed value

Section titled “Store one snapshot in one typed value”

This lesson records the entire Wesnoth pointer path, not only the final gold number:

Why keep all four fields?

  • player changing means the root now reaches another object.
  • side changing can mean the active faction or match state changed.
  • gold_address is the exact destination a later action would touch.
  • gold is the value the learner actually observed.

Equality now asks a useful question: “Did the whole chain and its value remain the same?” It is stronger than comparing only the final address.

Two equal reads are useful, not magical

Section titled “Two equal reads are useful, not magical”

The tool captures twice and accepts the result only when both snapshots agree:

This is a small optimistic consistency check. The tool does not stop the game. It assumes a short read will usually see a quiet moment, then checks that assumption.

⚠️ Two equal reads are not a mathematical proof that no intermediate state existed. They are a practical gate for a tiny offline lab. A debugger pause, a game-provided snapshot API, or a version counter is stronger when a larger structure must be perfectly atomic.

Alternative: Think of looking both ways before crossing: if both looks agree, the road is probably quiet, but a car could still appear. Equal reads raise confidence, not certainty.

The retry cap matters too. A loop that waits forever for stability can make a broken tool look frozen.

Capabilities follow the chosen action

Section titled “Capabilities follow the chosen action”

The command has two modes:

The program decides whether it needs write rights before opening the process:

This is capability-oriented design in plain English: if the user asked only to look, the handle should be unable to write.

Validate, write, verify, and recover

Section titled “Validate, write, verify, and recover”

The write path has three gates:

  1. re-capture and require the same snapshot;
  2. write exactly four little-endian bytes to the verified gold field;
  3. read the field back and require the requested result.

In the code below, observed is the snapshot the caller approved. A fresh snapshot must match it before any write; afterward, a read-back must equal replacement. Each added line enforces one arrow in the diagram.

The original helper writes to the gold address in a previously captured snapshot, then reports success. The target may have changed since that snapshot; the function also never checks what was stored.

A guarded action checks its precondition immediately before writing and its postcondition afterward. Matching snapshots reduce stale-address mistakes; they still cannot prevent the game changing between the check and the write.

Improved code

Show the diff

Takeaway: recheck the state you approved, then verify the result of the write.

This is not a database transaction: Windows cannot automatically roll back the game. It is a guarded action with a checked precondition and postcondition. That pattern also fits toggles, patches, save editors, configuration tools, and mod installers.

Narration: Without the final read-back, a tool could print success after a write that did not stick, for example if the game rewrote the value. Checking catches that.

Complete buildable tool

Section titled “Complete buildable tool”

The code below is the complete binary used by the lesson.

Complete lab source: snapshot_pipeline.rs

snapshot_pipeline.rs

windows-labs/src/bin/ · Rust, 121 lines

View on GitHub ↗

Show the codeHide the code
#[cfg(windows)]
fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    use anyhow::Context;
    use gha_windows_labs::Process;

    const PLAYER_ROOT: usize = 0x017E_ED18;
    const GAME_OFFSET: usize = 0x0A90;
    const GOLD_OFFSET: usize = 0x0004;
    const MAX_GOLD: u32 = 1_000_000;

    #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
    struct Snapshot {
        player: usize,
        side: usize,
        gold_address: usize,
        gold: u32,
    }

    fn pointer32(process: &Process, address: usize, label: &str) -> anyhow::Result<usize> {
        // 📏 Pointer width belongs to the 32-bit game, not to the Rust tool.
        let value = process
            .read_u32(address)
            .with_context(|| format!("could not read {label} at {address:#010x}"))?
            as usize;
        anyhow::ensure!(value != 0, "{label} was null; start a local match first");
        Ok(value)
    }

    fn capture(process: &Process) -> anyhow::Result<Snapshot> {
        // 🧭 Resolve every address with checked arithmetic before reading it.
        let player = pointer32(process, PLAYER_ROOT, "player root")?;
        let side_pointer = player
            .checked_add(GAME_OFFSET)
            .context("player + game offset overflowed")?;
        let side = pointer32(process, side_pointer, "current side")?;
        let gold_address = side
            .checked_add(GOLD_OFFSET)
            .context("side + gold offset overflowed")?;
        let gold = process.read_u32(gold_address)?;

        Ok(Snapshot {
            player,
            side,
            gold_address,
            gold,
        })
    }

    fn stable_snapshot(process: &Process) -> anyhow::Result<Snapshot> {
        for attempt in 1..=5 {
            let first = capture(process)?;
            let second = capture(process)?;
            if first == second {
                return Ok(first);
            }
            eprintln!("snapshot attempt {attempt} changed while it was being read; retrying");
        }
        anyhow::bail!("Wesnoth state did not stay stable for two consecutive captures")
    }

    let mut arguments = std::env::args().skip(1);
    let replacement = match arguments.next().as_deref() {
        None => None,
        Some("--set") => Some(
            arguments
                .next()
                .context("--set requires a gold value")?
                .parse::<u32>()
                .context("gold must be an unsigned decimal number")?,
        ),
        Some(other) => anyhow::bail!("unknown argument {other:?}; use no argument or --set GOLD"),
    };
    anyhow::ensure!(arguments.next().is_none(), "too many arguments");
    if let Some(value) = replacement {
        anyhow::ensure!(
            value <= MAX_GOLD,
            "gold exceeds the lab limit of {MAX_GOLD}"
        );
    }

    // 🔒 Read-only mode never requests VM_WRITE or VM_OPERATION rights.
    let process = Process::open_by_name("wesnoth.exe", replacement.is_some())?;
    anyhow::ensure!(
        process.is_32_bit()?,
        "this profile requires 32-bit Wesnoth 1.14.9"
    );
    let observed = stable_snapshot(&process)?;

    println!("Stable Wesnoth snapshot:");
    println!("  player:      {:#010x}", observed.player);
    println!("  side:        {:#010x}", observed.side);
    println!("  gold address:{:#010x}", observed.gold_address);
    println!("  gold:        {}", observed.gold);

    if let Some(value) = replacement {
        // ⚠️ The game kept running after observation. Rebuild the whole pointer
        // path and require the exact same evidence immediately before writing.
        let current = stable_snapshot(&process)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            current == observed,
            "state changed after confirmation; nothing was written"
        );
        process.write_u32(observed.gold_address, value)?;

        // ✅ Read back the postcondition instead of assuming the write succeeded.
        let written = process.read_u32(observed.gold_address)?;
        anyhow::ensure!(
            written == value,
            "read-back value was {written}, expected {value}"
        );
        println!("Changed gold from {} to {written}.", observed.gold);
    } else {
        println!("Observation only. Run with `--set GOLD` for the guarded local-lab write.");
    }
    Ok(())
}

#[cfg(not(windows))]
fn main() {
    eprintln!("This live snapshot pipeline must run on Windows.");
}

The same source is available as snapshot_pipeline.rs.

Build and run against Wesnoth

Section titled “Build and run against Wesnoth”
Windows VM

Use the exact 32-bit Wesnoth 1.14.9 course build, start a disposable local match, and build the Windows binary:

Confirm that the printed address and value match Cheat Engine or x64dbg. Then perform one explicit change:

The visible gold should become 888. End the match and run it again: the tool should report a null or unstable object instead of writing to address zero.

Read failures as information

Section titled “Read failures as information”
Failure What it means Correct response
Player root is null No supported local match is ready Start the match; do not invent an address
Snapshot keeps changing The pointer path changes between captures Stop after the retry cap
Architecture is not 32-bit This profile does not describe the target Refuse the run
State differs before write The earlier snapshot is out of date Write nothing and capture again
Read-back differs The requested postcondition was not reached Report failure; do not print success

A trustworthy tool has more useful stop paths than force paths. 🛡️

Extend the architecture

Section titled “Extend the architecture”

Once this pipeline is clear, try these controlled upgrades:

  • add a target-profile name and executable hash to the snapshot;
  • attach a timestamp and module base to each capture;
  • replace two reads with a game-owned frame counter when one is known;
  • make Action::Observe and Action::SetGold(u32) an enum;
  • unit-test decision logic with fake snapshots, without opening a process.

Keep remote I/O at the edge. The middle of the program should compare ordinary typed values.

What the write gate establishes

Section titled “What the write gate establishes”

The snapshot carries player and side identity along with gold and its address, so a changed object path invalidates a proposed action. Two equal captures are a bounded consistency check, not a lock on the running game. Observation mode therefore keeps a read-only handle. When an action is requested, a fresh precondition check guards the only write, and a read-back checks its postcondition before the tool reports success.

Lesson 4.4

Coordinates, Vectors, and Directions

A map tells us which places exist. Coordinates let a tool compare those places: where is the player, how far away is an enemy, and which way does a movement point? Begin with two positions on a grid, then turn their difference into distance and direction. The same operations work in two dimensions or three.

Extend 2D coordinates to three dimensions

Section titled “Extend 2D coordinates to three dimensions”

A 2D game often describes a position with x and y.

Picture a player at (2, 3) on that map and an enemy at (5, 7). The enemy is 3 units farther along x and 4 along y. Those differences form an arrow from the player to the enemy. Its straight-line length is 5: a right triangle with sides 3 and 4 has a long side of √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5.

A 3D game adds a third axis. If the enemy is also 12 units above the player, the arrow becomes (3, 4, 12) and its length becomes √(3² + 4² + 12²) = √169 = 13. The same subtraction and distance idea grew by one coordinate; no new kind of measurement was required.

TL;DR: Subtract two positions to get an arrow between them, and its length is the distance. A third axis changes nothing about the method.

This interactive lab needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it still explains the same idea.

That arrow turns positions into useful questions: how far away is a target, which direction should a character move, and is the target inside a guard’s view? We will use the same spatial language for automation and NPC decisions. The later camera lessons extend it to projecting the world onto a screen.

Rust can store the three numbers together:

Each field is an f32, a 32-bit floating-point number that can hold fractions as well as whole coordinates. #[derive(...)] asks Rust to generate conveniences such as copying and printing this small record; none of those traits changes the geometry. A Vec3 is not special hardware. It is a vector: an ordered group of numbers that we choose to treat as one mathematical object. The order matters because each slot has a role. Swapping x and z changes the meaning even when the three numbers stay the same.

Vectors are useful because one operation can apply to the whole idea. Adding a movement vector to a position moves the position. Subtracting two positions gives the difference between them.

Games disagree about which axis means “up.” Never assume. Move in one direction at a time and observe which field changes.

Note

🧭 Coordinate check: change one axis while keeping the others still. The field that follows the movement tells you what that axis means in this game.

Position versus direction

Section titled “Position versus direction”

A position answers “where?” A direction answers “which way?” Both can use three numbers, but they mean different things.

Self inside impl Vec3 means Vec3; self is the vector whose method was called. The subtraction uses enemy minus player, so the result points from the player to the enemy. length() squares each difference, adds the three squares, and takes the square root. These exact coordinates produce the (3, 4, 12) arrow and distance 13 calculated above. Reversing the operands would point the arrow backward while leaving its length unchanged. The :? in println! uses the Debug implementation generated for Vec3, so the program prints all three fields alongside the distance. Put this block after the Vec3 declaration to run the example.

A point and a direction can both be stored as three floats, but the allowed math is different:

Expression Meaning
point − point direction and distance between places
point + direction a new place after moving
direction + direction combined movement
point + point usually has no useful geometric meaning

This is a good example of why a memory layout does not tell the whole story. Three adjacent floats could be a position, velocity, color, scale, or Euler angles. Watch how the game uses them before assigning a name.

Length, normalization, and alignment

Section titled “Length, normalization, and alignment”

The length of a direction is its distance. Normalizing divides by that length so the result keeps only direction and has length one. Check for a near-zero length first; there is no meaningful direction from a point to itself.

For (3, 4, 0), length is 5, so the returned vector is Some((0.6, 0.8, 0)): it points the same way and its length is 1. Option expresses the case where no usable direction exists. When the points coincide, division by zero cannot produce a meaningful aim direction, so the function returns None rather than letting invalid numbers spread into later camera calculations. is_finite also rejects infinity and NaN from a damaged or stale snapshot.

The dot product measures alignment. For two normalized directions it is near 1 when they face the same way, 0 when perpendicular, and -1 when opposite. A field-of-view test can compare the camera’s forward direction with the direction to a target. This avoids turning both vectors into angles merely to ask whether they point roughly the same way.

For vectors a = (aₓ, aᵧ, a_z) and b = (bₓ, bᵧ, b_z):

That second line is why a dot product can become an angle with acos(clamp(dot, -1, 1)). Clamp first because floating-point rounding can produce 1.0000001, which is outside the mathematical input range of acos.

Worked through, a field-of-view test is three multiplications and two additions. Suppose the camera faces straight along positive x, and a target sits ahead and a little to the side:

0.8 is the cosine of roughly 37 degrees, so the target sits about 37 degrees off the centre of view. If visibility accepts directions at most 45 degrees from the centre of view, you never need acos at all: compare the dot product against cos(45°), which is about 0.707, and anything above that threshold is inside the cone. Comparing cosines is cheaper than converting to angles, and it sidesteps the rounding trap described above.

Alternative: Think of two people pointing: the dot product is 1 when they point the same way, 0 at right angles, and minus 1 when they point opposite ways.

Blending values: interpolation, easing, and following

Section titled “Blending values: interpolation, easing, and following”

Subtracting positions gives a direction. The reverse question is just as common: given two values, what is the value some fraction of the way between them? A character walks from one tile to the next, a colour fades, a camera slides toward a target. The answer is linear interpolation, usually called lerp. Start at a and add the fraction t, from 0 to 1, of the way to b:

p=a+(b−a) tp = a + (b - a)\,tp=a+(b−a)t

At t = 0 the result is a, at t = 1 it is b, and at t = 0.25 it is a quarter of the way. For numbers, a = 2 and b = 10 give 2 + (10 − 2) × 0.25 = 4. For a vector, blend each coordinate on its own: from (2, 3) to (5, 7), halfway (t = 0.5) is (2 + 3 × 0.5, 3 + 4 × 0.5) = (3.5, 5). A colour is three numbers too, so a half blend of red rgb(255, 0, 0) and blue rgb(0, 0, 255) is (127.5, 0, 127.5), which a display stores as rgb(128, 0, 128), a purple.

Lesson 4.1 left 3.33 ms over after a 16.67 ms step, so t = 3.33 ÷ 16.67 = 0.2. If a ball’s x was 794 after the earlier step and 796.5 after the later one, the picture shows 794 + (796.5 − 794) × 0.2 = 794.5. That is the blend the engine uses to draw motion between its steps.

Easing

Section titled “Easing”

A straight lerp moves at one speed, so it starts and stops abruptly. Easing reshapes t before it is used, so the motion can begin gently, end gently, or both. Here are four reshapings, with the value each gives at five moments:

Curve Formula t = 0 t = 0.25 t = 0.5 t = 0.75 t = 1
linear t 0 0.25 0.5 0.75 1
ease in (starts slowly) t × t 0 0.0625 0.25 0.5625 1
ease out (ends slowly) 1 − (1 − t)² 0 0.4375 0.75 0.9375 1
smoothstep (both ends) 3t² − 2t³ 0 0.15625 0.5 0.84375 1

Take an object that moves from x = 0 to x = 100 in one second. A quarter of the way through, the linear curve has put it at 25, the ease-in curve at 6.25 (it is still getting started), the ease-out curve at 43.75 (it is already slowing), and smoothstep at 15.625. Every curve starts at 0 and ends at 1, so every one reaches the same place; they differ in how they get there.

Following a moving target

Section titled “Following a moving target”

A camera or a character that chases a target can close a fraction of the remaining gap on every update:

With a gap of 10 and k = 0.2, the gap after each update is 10, then 10 × 0.8 = 8, then 6.4, then 5.12, then 4.096. The follower moves fast while it is far away and slows as it arrives, which looks smooth.

One fixed k has a flaw: a game running 120 updates a second closes the gap twice as often as one running 60. The fix is to tie k to the time that passed. With a stiffness s per second, use k = 1 − e^(−s × dt). For s = 10:

  • at 60 updates a second, dt = 1/60, so k = 1 − e^(−0.1667) = 1 − 0.8465 = 0.1535;
  • at 120 updates a second, dt = 1/120, so k = 1 − e^(−0.0833) = 1 − 0.9200 = 0.0800.

Two 120-per-second updates leave (1 − 0.0800)² ≈ 0.8465 of the gap, the same as one 60-per-second update, so the camera follows the same way on either machine.

Past the two samples: extrapolation

Section titled “Past the two samples: extrapolation”

The lerp formula does not forbid a t above 1. With t = 1.5 it continues the same line beyond b, and that is extrapolation: a guess about a value past the last one known. A game needs it when its newest information is already old. A client that receives another player’s position 10 times a second, every 0.10 s, still draws 60 pictures a second. Between two updates it can show a past state that lies between two known points (interpolation), or guess the present from the last two (extrapolation).

Take an update of x = 100 at 0.00 s and one of x = 106 at 0.10 s, so the speed is (106 − 100) ÷ 0.10 = 60 units a second. At 0.15 s, t = (0.15 − 0.00) ÷ 0.10 = 1.5, and the guess is 100 + (106 − 100) × 1.5 = 109. Now suppose the player stopped at 106, and the update for 0.20 s says so. The interpolated view draws the state from 0.10 s earlier, so both neighbouring updates are always known:

ExampleA player who stops at x = 106

Draw time Where the player is Interpolated view (shows the state 0.10 s earlier) Extrapolated view (the newest two updates)
0.10 s 106 state at 0.00 s: 100, late by 6 106
0.15 s 106 state at 0.05 s: 100 + 6 × 0.5 = 103, late by 3 106 + 60 × 0.05 = 109, 3 too far
0.19 s 106 state at 0.09 s: 100 + 6 × 0.9 = 105.4, late by 0.6 106 + 60 × 0.09 = 111.4, 5.4 too far
0.20 s 106 state at 0.10 s: 106 the update arrives, the speed is 0, and the view shows 106

The interpolated view is always behind the truth, by 0.10 s here, but it only ever shows places the player really was. The extrapolated view is never behind, but when the guess is wrong it overshoots and then snaps back: from 111.4 to 106 in one frame. When you read another player’s position from a client’s memory, the value may be one of these display values rather than the server’s own (Chapter 8).

Narration: That is why a smooth enemy on screen can be slightly behind, or briefly ahead of, where the server says it is: the client hides the gaps between updates.

Curves through several points

Section titled “Curves through several points”

A path that turns smoothly, such as a camera flight or the arc of a thrown item, is built from curves called splines. The simplest piece is a quadratic Bézier curve. It starts at P0, ends at P2, and is pulled toward a control point P1 without reaching it:

B(t)=(1−t)2P0+2(1−t) t P1+t2P2B(t) = (1 - t)^2 P_0 + 2(1 - t)\,t\,P_1 + t^2 P_2B(t)=(1−t)2P0​+2(1−t)tP1​+t2P2​

For P0 = (0, 0), P1 = (5, 10), and P2 = (10, 0), the point halfway along is 0.25 × (0, 0) + 0.5 × (5, 10) + 0.25 × (10, 0) = (2.5 + 2.5, 5) = (5, 5). The curve rises to 5 even though the control point is at 10. Longer paths chain many such pieces so that each one starts where the last ended, heading the same way; that is what a cubic spline does.

Blending turning angles needs more care than blending positions, because 350° and 10° are only 20° apart. Lesson 7.1 shows how orientations are blended.

Bounding volumes: distance as a contact test

Section titled “Bounding volumes: distance as a contact test”

The length of a direction is a distance, and a distance answers a contact question. Games give objects cheap stand-in shapes, called bounding volumes, and test those instead of the full model. The simplest is a circle (a sphere in 3D). Two circles touch when the distance between their centres is less than the sum of their radii.

Use the player at (2, 3) and the enemy at (5, 7) from earlier in this lesson. Their distance is 5, and its square is 3² + 4² = 25. With both radii 2, the sum is 4 and 4² = 16. Since 25 is more than 16, the circles do not touch. With radii 2 and 3.5 the sum is 5.5 and 5.5² = 30.25, which is more than 25, so they do. Comparing squared values gives the same answer without the square root.

A box that stays lined up with the axes is stored as its smallest and largest corner. Two such boxes overlap only if their ranges overlap on every axis. Box A spans x from 0 to 4 and y from 0 to 3, and box B spans x from 3 to 7 and y from 2 to 6. The x ranges share 3 to 4, and the y ranges share 2 to 3, so the boxes overlap. Move B to span x from 5 to 9 and they no longer do: 4 is less than 5, so one axis is enough to rule out contact.

These cheap tests are why a game’s collision tests can differ from its pictures, as Lesson 1.3 noted. Lesson 7.5 tests rays against such shapes, and Lesson 7.2 uses them to skip drawing things that are out of view.

From geometry to an action

Section titled “From geometry to an action”

A position names a place. Subtracting two positions gives a direction with a length; normalizing keeps only the direction. A dot product compares alignment, which lets a decision ask whether a target lies inside a view cone without calculating its angle first. Interpolation blends two values by a fraction, easing reshapes that fraction, and a bounding volume turns a distance into a contact test. Keep the coordinate meanings and units consistent before using any of these results.

From Coordinates to Target Selection now finds positions in an offline game and uses copied, validated values to choose an action.

Lesson 4.5

Maps as Grids of Game State

A player record is one object. A map asks the same memory question thousands of times: which tile is this, and what does this player know about it? In a Wesnoth match, terrain and visibility may describe the same location but live in different layers of state. Coordinates give us a way to relate them.

A map is usually a grid

Section titled “A map is usually a grid”

A rectangular map can be flattened into a one-dimensional array:

This interactive lab needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it still explains the same idea.

Make the conversion checked so an invalid tile cannot silently wrap:

On a three-column, two-row map, tile (2, 1) becomes index 1 × 3 + 2 = 5. Tile (3, 1) is outside the map and returns None. The checked multiplication also refuses dimensions so large that the index would overflow usize.

TL;DR: A flat list can hold a grid: a tile’s index is its row times the width plus its column. Check the bounds before you use it.

Never trust coordinates from remote memory until they pass bounds checks.

A grid needs a coordinate contract

Section titled “A grid needs a coordinate contract”

The formula only works after you know what x, y, width, and the base address mean. Games may store rows from top to bottom or bottom to top, pad each row, split terrain and visibility into separate layers, or keep one visibility layer per team.

For a candidate grid, recover these facts separately:

  • origin: which tile is (0, 0);
  • axis direction: which way increasing x and y move;
  • stride: how many elements or bytes separate two rows;
  • element width: how many bytes represent one tile;
  • layer: terrain, occupancy, visibility, or another property;
  • owner: global map state or one player’s derived view.

If the row stride includes padding, y * width + x is wrong even when the first row looks perfect. The byte address becomes base + y * row_stride + x * element_size. Verify it with tiles on different rows and near both edges of the map.

Visibility is often a derived view of terrain, units, teams, and line-of-sight checks for range and blocking terrain. A cached visibility layer can be useful to read without being the source of truth, because the game rebuilds it from those inputs. What matters is which system recomputes it and when.

Alternative: Think of fog as a sheet of tracing paper over the map: the terrain underneath is shared, but each player has their own sheet showing what they have seen.

Find one known tile

Section titled “Find one known tile”

In an offline Wesnoth match, compare a currently visible tile with a tile hidden by fog. Search for the observed visibility value, reveal or hide the tile through normal gameplay, and filter again.

Repeat with several tiles. You are testing whether candidates belong to:

  • one tile;
  • one row;
  • one player’s visibility layer;
  • a cached drawing value;
  • the authoritative map state.

Break on a normal update

Section titled “Break on a normal update”

Set a write breakpoint on a confirmed tile and move a unit so visibility updates.

Look for:

  • a base pointer to map data;
  • row or column math;
  • a player or team index;
  • the value written for hidden, explored, and visible states.

Do not assume a value such as 0xFFFF_FFFF means “visible.” It may mean -1, a bit mask, or an uninitialized sentinel. Collect examples for every state you name.

Model visibility as states

Section titled “Model visibility as states”

Suppose repeated observations show 0 for hidden tiles, 1 for explored tiles, and 2 for visible tiles in this exact build. Decode those raw values into named states so later code cannot confuse visibility with terrain. Keep every other number as Unknown until it has been investigated.

Keep Unknown. Silently treating a new value as visible would hide the fact that the byte has a state the model does not know about.

Narration: A value you did not expect is information: it may be a state you have not met yet. Keeping Unknown makes the surprise visible instead of hiding it.

Read a bounded layer

Section titled “Read a bounded layer”

Give the reader a verified layer base and map dimensions. It first checks width × height, caps the tile count, copies four bytes per tile from the game process, then decodes each copied u32 with the mapping above. The result is an owned vector of visibility states, not a pointer into live game memory.

The unwrap is safe here because chunks_exact(4) guarantees every chunk has four bytes, but an explicit conversion helper can make that invariant clearer in shared code.

Prefer an external visualization

Section titled “Prefer an external visualization”

Instead of patching the game, print a small text map or draw a separate window for your local lab:

That keeps the experiment observable and easy to shut down.

Reproduce the original Wesnoth map patch

Section titled “Reproduce the original Wesnoth map patch”

The original course called this exercise the map hack.

For Wesnoth 1.14.9, the write-breakpoint trail leads to 0x006CD519. The original eight-byte sequence updates a visibility column.

This build does not store one u32 per tile the way the model earlier in this lesson does. It packs 32 tiles into a single 32-bit column, one bit per tile, so the instructions below are bit-level field assignment rather than the y * width + x array indexing shown above. mov eax, ebp then shl eax, cl builds a single set bit, shifted into the position cl names — the bit that belongs to one specific tile in that column. not eax flips every bit, which turns that into a mask that is 0 at the tile’s position and 1 everywhere else. and dword ptr [esi], eax applies the mask to the stored column, clearing only that one tile’s visibility bit while leaving the other 31 alone. Replacing that full span with the following bytes forces the column bits to 1 using or [esi], 0xFF:

The observation, grid model, and debugger experiment above are the core exercise here. For an automated repeat after Lesson 8.3 teaches patch ownership and DLL lifecycle, the verified patch object expresses the same byte check and restoration in code:

Move a unit in a local match. As each visibility column is updated, every bit becomes 0xFFFF_FFFF, revealing the map as shown above. Call patch.restore() and start a fresh map to confirm fog behaves normally again.

The expected bytes are no longer an unnamed profile placeholder: they encode the four instructions shown in the debugger. The injected implementation is enable_wesnoth_map_reveal. After injection, F3 toggles it and End restores it.

//! Additional Wesnoth 1.14.9 hacks from the original map/stat lessons.

#![cfg(target_arch = "x86")]

use std::ptr;

use anyhow::Result;

use super::{LocalPatch, near_call, near_jump};

const PLAYER_ROOT: usize = 0x017E_ED18;
const GAME_OFFSET: usize = 0x0A90;
const SECOND_PLAYER_GOLD_OFFSET: usize = 0x0274;

const STAT_HOOK: usize = 0x005E_D129;
const STAT_PRINT_FUNCTION: usize = 0x005E_9630;
const STAT_RESUME: usize = 0x005E_D12E;

const MAP_UPDATE: usize = 0x006C_D519;

fn decimal_bytes(mut value: u32) -> [u8; 4] {
    value = value.min(999);
    let mut bytes = [0_u8; 4];
    if value >= 100 {
        bytes[0] = b'0' + (value / 100) as u8;
        bytes[1] = b'0' + ((value / 10) % 10) as u8;
        bytes[2] = b'0' + (value % 10) as u8;
    } else if value >= 10 {
        bytes[0] = b'0' + (value / 10) as u8;
        bytes[1] = b'0' + (value % 10) as u8;
    } else {
        bytes[0] = b'0' + value as u8;
    }
    bytes
}

extern "C" fn prepend_second_player_gold(edx: usize) {
    if edx == 0 {
        return;
    }
    // SAFETY: all addresses are from the verified 32-bit Wesnoth profile. Each
    // normal missing-match pointer is checked before the next dereference.
    let player = unsafe { ptr::read_volatile(PLAYER_ROOT as *const u32) } as usize;
    if player == 0 {
        return;
    }
    // SAFETY: the player record stores a game/side pointer at +0xA90.
    let game = unsafe { ptr::read_volatile((player + GAME_OFFSET) as *const u32) } as usize;
    if game == 0 {
        return;
    }
    // SAFETY: the second player's gold is the four-byte field at +0x274.
    let gold = unsafe { ptr::read_volatile((game + SECOND_PLAYER_GOLD_OFFSET) as *const u32) };
    // EDX points to the game's pointer to its output text buffer.
    // SAFETY: this shape was observed at the exact hooked print call.
    let output = unsafe { ptr::read_volatile(edx as *const u32) } as usize;
    if output == 0 {
        return;
    }
    let digits = decimal_bytes(gold);
    // SAFETY: the original course cave writes exactly the first three bytes of
    // this existing text buffer; the fourth byte in `digits` is only padding.
    unsafe {
        ptr::copy_nonoverlapping(digits.as_ptr(), output as *mut u8, 3);
    }
}

#[unsafe(naked)]
unsafe extern "C" fn wesnoth_stat_cave() {
    core::arch::naked_asm!(
        "pushfd",
        "pushad",
        "push edx",
        "call {prepend}",
        "add esp, 4",
        "popad",
        "popfd",
        // Replay the five-byte print call replaced by the detour.
        "call {original}",
        "jmp {resume}",
        prepend = sym prepend_second_player_gold,
        original = const STAT_PRINT_FUNCTION,
        resume = const STAT_RESUME,
    );
}

pub fn install_wesnoth_stat_hook() -> Result<LocalPatch> {
    let expected = near_call(STAT_HOOK, STAT_PRINT_FUNCTION)?;
    let cave = wesnoth_stat_cave as *const () as usize;
    let replacement = near_jump(STAT_HOOK, cave)?;
    LocalPatch::apply(STAT_HOOK, &expected, &replacement)
}

pub fn enable_wesnoth_map_reveal() -> Result<LocalPatch> {
    // mov eax,ebp ; shl eax,cl ; not eax ; and dword ptr [esi],eax
    const ORIGINAL: [u8; 8] = [0x8B, 0xC5, 0xD3, 0xE0, 0xF7, 0xD0, 0x21, 0x06];
    // nop/nop/nop ; or dword ptr [esi],0xFFFFFFFF ; nop/nop
    const REVEAL: [u8; 8] = [0x90, 0x90, 0x90, 0x83, 0x0E, 0xFF, 0x90, 0x90];
    LocalPatch::apply(MAP_UPDATE, &ORIGINAL, &REVEAL)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::decimal_bytes;

    #[test]
    fn formats_the_three_bytes_used_by_the_course_cave() {
        assert_eq!(&decimal_bytes(7)[..3], b"7\0\0");
        assert_eq!(&decimal_bytes(42)[..3], b"42\0");
        assert_eq!(&decimal_bytes(999)[..3], b"999");
    }
}

What the grid model teaches

Section titled “What the grid model teaches”

Fog of war is a per-player view over shared map data. The experiment shows how a grid and per-player visibility state can be represented; a different build may pack the same relationship into different bytes.

Lesson 4.6

Automation as a Feedback Loop

In a Wyrmsun local match, a bot that presses Recruit whenever gold is high could queue several workers before the first purchase appears on screen. A useful macro needs to know whether it has requested an action, whether the game accepted it, and when to stop trying.

A macro is not “press keys forever”

Section titled “A macro is not “press keys forever””

A reliable macro knows what state it is in, which condition allows the next step, and when to stop.

For Wyrmsun 5.0.1 in a local match, use this loop:

Every arrow has a reason. That is much easier to debug than nested if statements and sleeps.

This interactive lab needs JavaScript. The lesson text around it still explains the same idea.

Find the action, then find what it requires

Section titled “Find the action, then find what it requires”

The offline Wyrmsun 5.0.1 debugger trace reaches a unit-creation call:

Do not call an internal function based on one breakpoint. Several normal calls, watched in the debugger, show its:

  • required thread;
  • argument meaning;
  • object lifetimes;
  • return or error signal;
  • resource checks;
  • cooldown or event requirements.

An action that works once under the debugger may fail when called at the wrong time.

Automation is a closed feedback loop

Section titled “Automation is a closed feedback loop”

An open-loop macro sends inputs and assumes they worked. A reliable test bot closes the loop by observing the result:

These stages have different jobs:

Stage Question
Sense What does the current snapshot report?
Validate Is it complete, current, and plausible?
Decide Which single action is allowed by the policy?
Act How is that one request sent through the validated adapter?
Confirm Did game state change in the expected way?
Correct Should the bot retry, choose another state, or stop?

The sleep between ticks only limits the rate. It does not prove success. Menus, animation locks, pauses, missed input, and object replacement can all make an action request produce no outcome. Keep “requested recruit” separate from “worker count increased,” and never treat the first as proof of the second.

TL;DR: A reliable bot closes the loop: sense, act once, then check the result before acting again. A sleep only limits the rate.

For testing, record snapshots and feed them through the decision function. The same sequence should produce the same decisions without launching the game.

Model states with an enum

Section titled “Model states with an enum”

The bot needs a state for each distinct obligation. Acting remembers that a recruitment was requested, Cooldown stores how long to wait after a confirmed action, and Recovering carries a reason for a failed one. A single enum value means the bot occupies only one of these states at a time.

Impossible combinations disappear. We cannot accidentally be both Acting and Cooldown.

Alternative: Think of a traffic light: it is red, amber or green, never two at once. An enum likewise represents exactly one bot state at a time.

Keep observations separate

Section titled “Keep observations separate”

The game snapshot below is a copy of facts the bot has validated, not the bot’s intention. next_state receives that copy, the current macro state, and a stop request. It chooses one next state without pressing a key or writing to the game. For example, Ready with at least 100 resources becomes Acting; it does not become Cooldown until a later snapshot confirms the action.

This transition function is safe, deterministic, and easy to test without a game.

Test the decision logic

Section titled “Test the decision logic”

Feed the transition function a ready, active snapshot with enough resources, then set stop to true. The expected result is Stopped, because a user stop must outrank a possible recruit action. The test pins that priority without launching Wyrmsun.

The low-level observation and action layers may be version-specific. The state machine should not be.

A reliable loop answers four questions

Section titled “A reliable loop answers four questions”

Before writing loop or while, state these four facts:

  1. Start: which state exists before the first tick?
  2. Continue: what must remain true for another tick to run?
  3. Progress: what changes so the loop does not repeat the same work forever?
  4. Stop: which event ends it, even if the game is paused or closes?

For this macro, the start is Waiting, each snapshot allows one transition, cooldown ticks count toward zero, and the shared stop request moves the machine to Stopped. A fixed sleep controls how often observations occur; it is not the thing that makes the logic correct.

Trace a few ticks before connecting the action adapter:

Current state Snapshot fact Next state Side effect
Waiting match and player ready Ready none
Ready resources are 120 Acting { attempt: 1 } request one action
Acting action confirmed Cooldown { ticks_left: 5 } none
any active state stop requested Stopped begin cleanup

If a row has two unrelated actions, the state probably owns too much work. If a row has no path to Stopped, the design is not safe to run yet.

Rate limits and stop behavior

Section titled “Rate limits and stop behavior”

Use a bounded tick rate, not a busy loop:

Before unloading an in-process library, set the stop flag, wait for the worker to exit, and restore any temporary state.

Narration: A worker thread still running when its library is unloaded would execute code that no longer exists, and the game would crash. Stopping it first avoids that.

Wire it to Wyrmsun 5.0.1 after the DLL lessons

Section titled “Wire it to Wyrmsun 5.0.1 after the DLL lessons”
Windows VM

You can complete the state-machine and recorded-snapshot tests above before loading code into a game. The pinned Wyrmsun port below is a deeper application to revisit after Lesson 8.3 teaches verified detours and Lesson 6.9 teaches the input worker. Its concrete addresses and hooks are retained here so the bot design can be compared with the original course’s running implementation.

This is the original course’s macro bot, rebuilt as an explicit state machine.

The original lab found these module-relative facts:

Purpose wyrmsun.exe offset
recruit-unit call target 0x2CF7
recruit-unit hook 0x223471
main-loop hook 0x385D34
main-loop call target 0xDBCA
gold-chain root 0x61A504

Wyrmsun relocates its module, so calculate module_base + offset every run. For one observed base of 0x00F40000, the recruit target became 0x00F42CF7 and the hook became 0x01163471.

The Cheat Engine gold path was:

Capture one legitimate worker record at the recruit hook (ecx points to the outer pointer) into a local 0x110-byte buffer. When gold is over 3000, copy that captured record back, put the expected pointer in ecx, and call the verified recruit function from the game-loop hook. The original three overwritten recruit instructions were push ecx, mov ecx, esi, and the call; replay all eight bytes before returning.

Build the DLL for the game’s 32-bit architecture, inject it into your offline match, recruit one worker normally to fill the buffer, then gather more than 3000 gold. Workers should begin recruiting automatically from the selected structure. If they do not, log the calculated module addresses and verify each original byte before allowing the hooks to install.

How the two Wyrmsun caves complete the action

Section titled “How the two Wyrmsun caves complete the action”

The complete implementation is in strategy_hooks.rs. It finds the relocated module, verifies both original call sequences, installs two detours, captures the legitimate 0x110-byte record, resolves the entire gold chain, calls the real recruit function with x86 thiscall, replays the removed game-loop call, and restores both hooks.
